For the truth is, one does a good deal of good when he does what the Scripture enjoins, "Go not after thy lusts;" yet he falls short of perfection, in that he fails to keep the great commandment, "Thou shalt not covet." The law said, "Thou shalt not covet," in order that, when we find ourselves lying in this diseased state, we might seek the medicine of Grace, and by that commandment know both in what direction our endeavours should aim as we advance in our present mortal condition, and to what a height it is possible to reach in the future immortality. For unless perfection could somewhere be attained, this commandment would never have been given to us.

There you are then, the law tells you "you shall not covet." You know the law which says, "You shall not covet." Covetousness surges up in you, which you didn't know. It was there inside, you see, but it wasn't known. You started to make an effort to overcome what was inside, and what was hidden came to light. Proud fellow, through the law you have been made into a transgressor. Acknowledge grace, and become a singer of praise.

Even a lion can be shooed off its prey by the terrifying threat of arms and weapons and the crowd of people perhaps surrounding it or coming to attack it; and yet the lion comes, the lion returns. It hasn't seized its prey; it hasn't either laid aside its evil intention. If that's what you're like, your justice is still the sort by which you take care not to get tortured. What's so great about being afraid of punishment? Who isn't afraid of it?

To save me from saying a lot, among other commandments it contains "You shall not covet your neighbor's property." Don't covet; don't go up and down in front of that country house belonging to someone else and sigh because it's such a fine one. Do not covet your neighbor's property. "The Lord's is the earth and its fullness." What haven't you acquired, if you have got hold of God? So don't covet your neighbor's property.

The Law of the Old Testament certainly forbids coveting another's wife, but it does not punish a king for commanding brave deeds of soldiers, or for desiring water. And we all know that David, pierced by the sword of concupiscence, both coveted and took away another man's wife. Fitting scourges followed his fault, and he corrected the evil he had perpetrated through the lamentations of penance.

But because the neighbor is an image of the Trinity, and to him, insofar as he bears the image of the Holy Spirit, benignity is owed: with respect to benignity, to which cupidity and concupiscence are opposed, each of which can be in deed or in heart, four are taken, namely thou shalt not commit adultery, thou shalt not covet thy neighbor's wife, thou shalt not steal, and thou shalt not covet another's goods. And these are to be ordered according to greater or lesser injuries by which justice can be violated. And thus the rules pertaining to the necessity of justice ought to be contained in the ten precepts.

Offense in the mind has two roots according to the twofold concupiscence, namely of the flesh and of the eyes. Against the concupiscence of the flesh there is one commandment: "Thou shalt not covet thy neighbor's wife." Against the concupiscence of the eyes there is another commandment: "nor his field, nor any other thing."

"You shall not covet your neighbor's goods, nor shall you desire his wife;" in which He prohibits the twofold concupiscence, namely of the eyes and of the flesh, which are the kindling of all evils and the root of all sins: because when the concupiscible power is infected and corrupted, it corrupts all the other powers of the soul. In the preceding commandments: "You shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, you shall not speak false testimony," every illicit exterior act committed against one's neighbor is prohibited. In these two: "You shall not covet your neighbor's goods, nor shall you desire his wife," the illicit interior act is prohibited, and here the concupiscence of the eyes, or covetousness, is prohibited, which "is the root of all evils"; the concupiscence of the flesh is also prohibited, which is the kindling of all sins. Through this twofold concupiscence occurs the transmission of all evils and sins; and therefore the divine law prohibits it, and in this prohibits all evils and all sins. This is the fever by which all the children of Adam are feverish, and which generates all evils.

The ninth plague was of darkness, by which the covetous and avaricious are struck, because nothing so blinds a man as covetousness. Whence the Prophet: "Gifts and presents blind the eyes of the prudent and change the words of the just;" Solomon: "Nothing is more wicked than the avaricious man. For he has even his own soul for sale, because in his life he has cast away his inmost parts."

The tenth plague was the death of the firstborn, by which the carnal are struck, like Esau. For the Apostle says: "Lest anyone among you be a fornicator, like Esau, and lose his birthright." Carnal concupiscence took from us our noble generation, by which we would all be born innocent and heirs of paradise, and it makes us be born in death and guilt and the loss of the birthright. This was prefigured in Reuben, who lost the right of the firstborn, because he went up to his father's bed and defiled his couch; and Joseph, on account of his chastity, was made prince over his brothers.

That which straightens all affective dispositions is as follows: You shall not covet your neighbor's wife, etc. As Augustine writes, "The law is good, for while prohibiting concupiscence, it also prohibits any evil." But concupiscence is twofold, of the flesh and of cupidity, and the latter is the root of all evil. Hence, in this commandment, the Lawgiver Himself went down to details such as the ass, the slave, the female servant, etc.

"You shall not covet your neighbor's goods." There is this difference between the divine and the human laws that human law judges only deeds and words, whereas the divine law judges also thoughts. The reason is because human laws are made by men who see things only exteriorly, but the divine law is from God, who sees both external things and the very interior of men. "You are the God of my heart" [Ps 72:26]. And again: "Man sees those things that appear, but the Lord sees the heart" [1 Sam 16:7]. Therefore, having considered those Commandments which concern words and deeds, we now treat of the Commandments about thoughts. For with God the intention is taken for the deed, and thus the words, "You shall not covet," mean to include not only the taking by act, but also the intention to take. Therefore, it says: "You shall not even covet your neighbor's goods." There are a number of reasons for this.

The first reason for the Commandment is that man's desire has no limits, because desire itself is boundless. But he who is wise will aim at some particular end, for no one should have aimless desires: "A covetous man shall not be satisfied with money" [Eccles 5:9]. But the desires of man are never satisfied, because the heart of man is made for God. Thus, says St. Augustine: "You have made us for You, O Lord, and our heart is restless until it rests in You." Nothing, therefore, less than God can satisfy the human heart: "He satisfies your desire with good things" [Ps 102:5].

The second reason is that covetousness destroys peace of heart, which is indeed highly delightful. The covetous man is ever solicitous to acquire what he lacks, and to hold that which he has: "The fullness of the rich will not suffer him to sleep" [Eccles 5:11]. "For where your treasure is, there is your heart also" [Mt 6:21]. It was for this, says St. Gregory, that Christ compared riches to thorns [Lk 8:14].

Thirdly, covetousness in a man of wealth renders his riches useless both to himself and to others, because he desires only to hold on to them: "Riches are not fitting for a covetous man and a niggard" [Sir 14:3]. The fourth reason is that it destroys the equality of justice: "Neither shall you take bribes, which even blind the wise, and pervert the words of the just" [Ex 23:8]. And again: "He who loves gold shall not be justified" [Sir 31:5]. The fifth reason is that it destroys the love of God and neighbor, for says St. Augustine: "The more one loves, the less one covets," and also the more one covets, the less one loves. "Nor despise your dear brother for the sake of gold" [Sir 7:20]. And just as "No man can serve two masters," so neither can he serve "God and mammon" [Mt 6:24].

Finally, covetousness produces all kinds of wickedness. It is "the root of all evil," says St. Paul, and when this root is implanted in the heart it brings forth murder and theft and all kinds of evil. "They that will become rich, fall into temptation, and into the snare of the devil, and into many unprofitable and hurtful desires which drown men in destruction and perdition. For the desire of money is the root of all evil" [1 Tim 6:9-10]. And note, furthermore, that covetousness is a mortal sin when one covets one's neighbor's goods without reason; and even if there be a reason, it is a venial sin.

St. John says in his first Epistle that "all that is in the world is the concupiscence of the flesh, the concupiscence of the eyes, and the pride of life" [1 Jn 2:16]. Now, all that is desirable is included in these three, two of which are forbidden by the precept: "You shall not covet your neighbor's house." Here "house," signifying height, refers to avarice, for "glory and wealth shall be in his house" [Ps 111:3]. This means that he who desires the house, desires honors and riches. And thus after the precept forbidding desire for the house of one's neighbor comes the Commandment prohibiting concupiscence of the flesh: "You shall not covet your neighbor's wife."

Because of the corruption which resulted from the Fall, none has been free from concupiscence except Christ and the glorious Virgin. And wherever there is concupiscence, there is either venial or mortal sin, provided that it is allowed to dominate the reason. Hence the precept is not, let sin not be; for it is written: "I know that nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh" [Rm 7:18].

First of all, sin rules in the flesh when, by giving consent to it, concupiscence reigns in the heart. And, therefore, St. Paul adds "so as to obey the lusts thereof" to the words: "Do not let sin reign in your mortal body" [Rm 6:12]. Accordingly the Lord says: "Whoever looks on a woman to lust after her, has already committed adultery with her in his heart" [Mt 5:28]. For with God the intention is taken for the act.

Secondly, sin rules in the flesh when the concupiscence of our heart is expressed in words: "Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks" [Mt 12:34]. And again: "Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth" [Eph 4:29]. Therefore, one is not without sin who composes frivolous songs. Even the philosophers so thought, and poets who wrote amatory verses were sent into exile. Lastly, sin rules in the flesh when at the behest of desire the members are made to serve iniquity: "As you have yielded your members to serve uncleanness to greater and greater iniquity" [Rm 6:19]. These, therefore, are the progressive steps of concupiscence.

We must realize that the avoidance of concupiscence demands much labor, for it is based on something within us. It is as hard as trying to capture an enemy in one's own household. However, this desire can be overcome in four ways.

Firstly, by fleeing the external occasions such as, for instance, bad company; and in fact whatever may be an occasion for this sin: "Do not gaze upon a maiden lest her beauty be a stumbling-block to you... Do not look around you in the ways of the city, nor wander up and down in its streets. Turn away your face from a woman dressed up, and do not gaze upon another's beauty. For many have perished by the beauty of a woman, whereby lust is enkindled as a fire" [Sir 9:5-9]. And again: "Can a man hide fire in his bosom, and his garments not burn?" [Prov 6:27]. And thus Lot was commanded to flee, "neither stay you in all the country about" [Gen 19:17].

The second way is by not giving an opening to thoughts which of themselves are the occasion of lustful desires. And this must be done by mortification of the flesh: "I chastise my body, and bring it into subjection" [1 Cor 9:27].

The third way is perseverance in prayer: "Unless the Lord build the house, they labor in vain who build it" [Ps 126:1]. And also: "I knew that I could not otherwise be continent, except God gave it" [Wis 8:21]. Again: "This kind is not cast out save by prayer and fasting" [Mt 17:21]. All this is not unlike a fight between two persons, one of whom you desire to win, the other to lose. You must sustain the one and withdraw all support from the other. So also between the spirit and the flesh there is a continual combat. Now, if you wish the spirit to win, you must assist it by prayer, and likewise you must resist the flesh by such means as fasting; for by fasting the flesh is weakened.

The fourth way is to keep oneself busy with wholesome occupations: "Idleness hath taught much evil" [Sir 33:29]. Again: "This was the iniquity of Sodom your sister, pride, fullness of bread, and abundance, and the idleness of her" [Ez 16:49]. St. Jerome says: "Be always busy in doing something good, so that the devil may find you ever occupied." Now, study of the Scriptures is the best of all occupations, as St. Jerome tells us: "Love to study the Scriptures and you will not love the vices of the flesh" [Ad Paulin.].

But to urge people to be content with what they haven't got is a piece of impudence hard for even the English poor to pardon. But though the creed of content is unsuited to certain special riddles and wrongs, it remains true for the normal of mortal life. We speak of divine discontent; discontent may sometimes be a divine thing, but content must always be the human thing. It may be true that a particular man, in his relation to his master or his neighbour, to his country or his enemies, will do well to be fiercely unsatisfied or thirsting for an angry justice. But it is not true, no sane person can call it true, that man as a whole in his general attitude towards the world, in his posture towards death or green fields, towards the weather or the baby, will be wise to cultivate dissatisfaction. In a broad estimate of our earthly experience, the great truism on the tablet remains: he must not covet his neighbour's ox nor his ass nor anything that is his. In highly complex and scientific civilisations he may sometimes find himself forced into an exceptional vigilance. But, then, in highly complex and scientific civilisations, nine times out of ten, he only wants his own ass back.
A Miscellany of Men: The Contented Man

AGAINST THE PAGANS. — The tradition of the pagans, having been invented by man, cannot be denied; but that our Law was given by God is an evident fact. For on the mountain the majesty of God appeared to give the Law to men. And that faith might be placed in this, He first sent many signs and wonders done in Egypt, which even today books testify to, stored by Ptolemy in the library of Alexandria. Therefore, then, He consented to give the Law, that no one might doubt that it was God who delivered it. For the majesty of God was seen openly and plainly by all, with such brilliance and terror that no other god besides Him was believed to exist, and that what He commanded was held worthy of all observance. And that all things might agree with the divine order, let the given Law be examined, to see whether there is anything unjust in it, anything dishonorable, anything ridiculous. Therefore it was fitting that God should be made known; not that He should appear in a corner by deceit, He who cannot be limited; nor in a mirror, where what is seen is other than it appears through enticing fraud; nor would He deliver precepts to be kept which, because they were dishonorable, would be performed in darkness. For since the knowledge of the one God had been obliterated in the world by the habit of sinning, because falsehood had supplied a veil for the truth, the merciful and gracious God, unwilling that His work should become accountable to destruction, consented to visit the human race. He did not appear as those did who wished falsely to be called gods; but as He is the Truth of God, so He revealed Himself, that He might remove the error which, by the proclamation of false gods, had corrupted the understanding of the world. In short, more than six hundred thousand men, having gone out of Egypt, seeing and knowing that this Lord was above all from the revealing of unspeakable glory, were afraid to approach Him, but from afar, with knees bent, they worshiped Him (Exod. 20:18). Afterwards, as other signs followed besides those which He had done in Egypt, in all these wonders He was revealed as the one God. These things became known in almost all tongues; these were a terror to neighboring nations. What such thing is there among the gods of the Gentiles? To what nation, to what people have they shown their glory? What signs or powers have they performed as testimony of their divinity? Where or when are they proved to have spoken?

But notice how it happened there and how it happened here. There, the people stood a long way off; there was an atmosphere of dread, not of love. I mean, they were so terrified that they said to Moses, "Speak to us yourself, and do not let the Lord speak to us, lest we die." So God came down, as it is written, on Sinai in fire; but he was terrifying the people who stood a long way off, and "writing with his finger on stone," not on the heart.Here, however, when the Holy Spirit came, the faithful were gathered together as one; and he didn't terrify them on a mountain but came in to them in a house. There came a sudden sound, indeed, from heaven, as of a fierce squall rushing upon them; it made a noise, but nobody panicked. You have heard the sound, now see the fire too, because each was there on the mountain also, both fire and sound; but there, there was smoke as well, here, though, the fire was clear. "There appeared to them," Scripture says, you see, "divided tongues, as of fire." Terrifying them from a long way off? Far from it. Because "it settled upon each one of them, and they began to talk in languages, as the Spirit gave them utterance." Hear a person speaking a language, and understand the Spirit writing not on stone but on the heart.

I dessire to open my month, my brethren, to speak on the elevated place of humility; but I am filled with fear, as a man who is conscious of the fact, that he will speak concerning God in a tale of his own speech. For humility is the garment of divinity; for the word which became man, put it on and spoke in it with us, through our body. And every one who puts it on in truth, by humility takes the likeness of Him that has descended from His height and concealed the splendour of His majesty and hidden His glory, lest the creation should perish by the sight of Him. For the creation was not able to see Him without His being united to a part of it which He should assume and speak with them through it, then the creation was able to hear the word of His mouth, face to face.

The children of Israel were not able to listen to His voice, while He spoke with them from within the cloud; then should the creation be able to bear the sight of Him openly? For the children of Israel were so troubled that they said to Moses: Let us speak with thee, and listen thou to His words for us; but let Him not speak with us, lest we die. And so terrible was the sight, that even the intermediary said: I fear and tremble. for on mount Sinai the splendour of His glory revealed itself, and the whole mountain smoked and was shaken from fear of His revelation that took place on it, so that even the beasts which approached the foot of the mountain, died. And all the children of Israel, on the order of Moses, prepared themselves, every one purifying himself for three days in order to be worthy of listening to the sound of God’s speech and of seeing His revelation. And when the moment came, they were not able to bear the sight of His light, and the vehemence of the sound of His thunder.

But now that He has poured out His grace on the world by His coming, not in earthquake nor in fire, nor with a terrible and vehement sound — but descending as the rain upon the lamb’s fleece, and as the soft dew drops which softly descend upon the earth — it has pleased Him to speak with us in a different way, concealing His majesty in the cover of flesh, speaking to us while being in us, in the garment which Providence had woven from the womb of the virgin, so that we, seeing Him speak with us as one of our race, should not be terrified by the sight of Him.

21: We read that every Hebrew keeps the same Passover, and that in the seventh year every prisoner is set free, and that at Jubilee, that is, the fiftieth year, every possession returns to its owner. All this refers not to the present but to the future. For being in bondage during the six days of this world, on the seventh day, the true and eternal sabbath, we shall be free. If we wish to be free, we will be free even while still in bondage in the world. If, however, we do not desire it, our ear will be bored in token of our disobedience. We shall, with our wives and children, remain in perpetual slavery if we prefer the flesh and its works to liberty.

That man is truly free, a true Hebrew, who is entirely God's. Everything that he possesses shares in freedom. He has nothing in common with the man who rejects freedom and says, "I have loved my master.… I will not go out free." The man who subjects himself to the world is returned not only to his master but also to his infirmity, because he loves the world or his mind, that is, his nous,the author of this desire. He is returned not only to his wife but even to those pleasures which make him so bound to household matters that he does not care for what is eternal. Thus "at his threshold and door his master shall pierce his ear," in order that he might remember the decision by which he chose slavery.

We must also inquire what difference there is between "age" and "age of the age," or "ages of ages," and where it is used for a short span of time, and where for eternity: for in Hebrew "age," that is, OLAM (עלם), when it has the letter VAV placed in it, signifies eternity, but when it is written without VAV, the fiftieth year, which they call the Jubilee. For this reason too that Hebrew who, because of his wife and children, loving his master, is subjected to servitude with his ear pierced, is ordered to serve "for ever" (in sæculum) (Exod. 21), that is, up to the fiftieth year. And the Moabites and Ammonites (Deut. 23) do not enter the church of the Lord up to the fifteenth generation, and "for ever": because every hard condition was dissolved at the coming of the Jubilee.

For there was a command under the law that cities of refuge should be appointed, in order that they who were sought after to be put to death might at least have some means of saving themselves. And when he who spoke to Moses, the Word of the Father, appeared in the end of the world, he also gave this commandment, saying, "But when they persecute you in this city, flee into another."

Even the person who unwittingly committed a murder was still within the ministry of God, since the law makes this statement regarding him: "God delivered him into his hands." His hands therefore served as an instrument of divine punishment. The Levite is then the minister who remits, whereas the man who (in the example just cited) unwittingly and unwillingly struck another in a homicidal act became in fact an administrator of divine punishment. See to it that Christ is infused into the act of slaying an impious man and that sanctification accompany and be part of your attempt to abolish what is abominable.

[Exodus 21:17] But ye say, Whosoever shall say to his father or his mother, It is a gift, by whatsoever thou mightest be profited by me;  And honour not his father or his mother, he shall be free. Thus have ye made the commandment of God of none effect by your tradition.

One who speaks ill of his mother or father will die the death. One who speaks well of them will have full enjoyment of the rewards of life. If our parents in the flesh should enjoy such good will from us, so much the more would this hold true for our parents in the spirit.

The man who is guilty of unintentional homicide has given sufficient satisfaction in eleven years. We shall, without doubt, observe what is laid down by Moses in the case of wounded men, and shall not hold a murder to have been committed in the case of a man who lies down after he has been struck, and walks again leaning on his staff. If, however, he does not rise again after he has been struck, nevertheless, from there being no intent to kill, the striker is a homicide, but an unintentional homicide.

Because the written law was a law of rigor, it not only approves the threefold obedience, but also punishes its transgressors. It punishes the rebellious servant, Exodus 21: He who strikes his servant or handmaid with a rod, if he survive for a day or two, he shall not be subject to penalty, because he is his property.

"But if two men should be fighting and strike a pregnant woman, and her infant should come forth not yet formed, he shall suffer loss, as much as the woman's husband shall impose, and he shall pay with honor. But if it be fully formed, he shall give life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot, burn for burn, wound for wound, bruise for bruise." First of all, in these matters, I think we must inquire under what heading of the law statutes of this kind are reckoned. For it is not, as it seems to the simpler sort, that everything which is enacted is called "law"; rather, some things are indeed called law, some testimonies, others commandments and acts of righteousness, and some are called judgments. This the eighteenth Psalm teaches more plainly, gathering them together in one place, when it says: "the law of the Lord is blameless, converting souls; the testimony of the Lord is faithful, granting wisdom to little ones. The acts of righteousness of the Lord are upright, gladdening hearts; the precept of the Lord is clear, enlightening the eyes. The fear of the Lord is chaste, enduring unto the age of the age; the judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves." Since, then, these diversities exist among the things enacted in the law, the passage now in hand is written under the heading of acts of righteousness or justifications. For thus it says above: "and these are the acts of righteousness which you shall set openly before them." But it is not for the present occasion to set forth the differences of each of these, for we are called upon to explain the things which have been read. It should indeed be known that some portion of these matters, of which we must treat, is set down in the Gospel according to Matthew, the Lord speaking in this manner: "you have heard that it was said: eye for eye, tooth for tooth. But I say to you, do not resist evil. But if anyone strike you on the right cheek, turn to him the other also." But perhaps one who reads the Scriptures more attentively may say that the words we have recalled as written in the Gospel are not taken from this passage of Exodus, but rather from Deuteronomy, where nonetheless certain things are recorded as written in this manner: "but if," it says, "an unjust witness should stand, bearing testimony against a man concerning impiety, both men who are in controversy shall be set before the Lord and before the priests and before the judges, whoever they may be in those days, and the judges shall examine diligently and investigate. And behold, they shall find that the unjust witness has testified unjustly, that he has risen up against his brother; and you shall do to him as he himself attempted to do to his brother, and you shall remove the malignant one from your midst, that the rest, hearing, may have fear, and may not go on further to do according to this evil word among you. Your eye shall not spare over him: life for life, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot." Similar things indeed seem to be said in both places; yet it is not plainly shown from which passage in particular the words set down in the Gospel seem to be taken, where he said: "you have heard that it was said: eye for eye, tooth for tooth."

Nevertheless, our discourse must now be turned to the things written in Exodus, where two men are fighting and strike a pregnant woman, and strike her in such a way that the infant comes forth from her either "already formed" or "not yet formed." First indeed let us consider concerning the one who has come forth "not yet formed": how is it that one of those who are fighting is commanded to be struck with a monetary loss, when by Scripture the guilt of the quarrel is referred not to one, but to both? What too is the meaning of the fact that the woman's husband "imposes" or lays it upon him and not upon them, and that he "shall pay" and not rather that they shall pay "with honor"? And what is this honor? But if the infant has come forth already formed, the pregnant woman having been struck by the fighting men, we easily understand that life is given for life, that is, that what was committed is avenged by death. But the things that follow are worth explaining: "eye for eye, tooth for tooth." For it does not seem possible that we should understand of the infant, which the struck woman has miscarried, even if it came forth formed, that it lost an eye in the womb, struck by the heel of a fighting man, for which he ought to be deprived of an eye by the judges. But grant that even this be so, since it is reported as already formed—what shall we say also about the tooth? Did it have teeth in the mother's womb, which the striker's blow could knock out? But if we refer these things to her who has miscarried, how again will it fit that a miscarrying woman should lose an eye or suffer pains in her teeth? But grant that she is said to be struck in the eye or in the tooth, and that from this the cause of casting out the infant arose; grant that she received a bruise, grant that she received a wound—what shall we say too about "burn for burn"? Could a woman standing by while men were fighting be burned, so that "burn for burn" be paid? Yet each of these particulars seems to me not to admit of an easy solution even in the passages of Deuteronomy, where similar things are recorded as written. For let us suppose there too that "an unjust witness has risen up" speaking false testimony against a man concerning impiety. Let both be brought to judgment, let the judges inquire diligently, let them detect that that accuser or witness has spoken falsely: how shall the judge, who ought not to spare the false witness and to condemn the life of the guilty party for the life of an innocent one—how, I say, shall he also be able to take out "eye for eye"? As though indeed the one who was being unjustly accused was to have been injured in his eye by the accuser, or in tooth or hand or foot. But these things have been said by us because we wish to show that in both passages the things written cannot easily be expounded. For it was fitting for us first to examine according to the history the things that are read, and thus, since "the law is spiritual," to seek the spiritual understanding in them.

But, as far as concerns the present, even that portion of allegory itself, which is always accustomed to lie more broadly open, is here forced into a narrow compass. Nevertheless, as far as we are able, we shall attempt to explain what seems to us in this passage. We have frequently said that in the Scriptures the members of the soul are named by the same words and the same functions by which the members of the body are used or called. For example, as when it is said: "you see the speck in your brother's eye, and behold, in your eye a beam lies beneath." For it is certain that he does not speak of the eye of the body, in which a beam lies, but of the eye of the soul. And when he says: "he who has ears to hear, let him hear," and: "how beautiful are the feet of those who bring good tidings of peace," and many things similar to these. Now we have set these things down beforehand for this reason, that the likeness in the names of the members may not disturb us. Let these two men, then, who are fighting, be two men disputing and inquiring with one another about the doctrines or questions of the law, and, to speak in the words of the Apostle, quarreling "about battles of words." Whence the same Apostle also, knowing that quarrels of this kind arise among brethren, gives command and says: "do not contend with words, for it is useful for nothing, unto the subversion of the hearers," and elsewhere: "but avoid the questions of the law, knowing that they beget quarrels. But the servant of God ought not to quarrel." Because, therefore, these men who quarrel over questions quarrel "unto the subversion of the hearers," for this reason they strike a pregnant woman and cast out her infant, whether already formed or not yet formed. The pregnant woman is said to be the soul which has recently conceived the word of God. Now concerning such a conception we read it written also in another place: "from fear of you, O Lord, we have conceived in the womb, and we have given birth." Those, therefore, who conceive and immediately give birth—these are to be reckoned not as women, but as men, and perfect men. Hear, finally, also the prophet saying: "if the earth has given birth in one day, and a nation has been born at once." This is the generation of the perfect, which is born immediately, on the same day, as soon as it has been conceived. But lest it seem new to you that we have said men give birth, we have already long since set forth how you ought to take the names of the members, that you may withdraw from bodily senses and grasp the understanding of the inner man. But if you wish that I satisfy you still further in this also from the Scriptures, hear the Apostle saying: "my little children, whom I again bring forth in travail, until Christ be formed in you." Perfect, therefore, and strong men are those who immediately, as soon as they conceive, give birth—that is, those who bring the conceived word of faith forth into works. But the soul which conceives and retains in the womb and does not give birth, this one is called a woman, just as the prophet also says: "the pains of childbirth have come upon her, and the power of giving birth is not in her." This soul, then, which now on account of its weakness is called a woman, when two men are quarreling with one another and in the contest bringing forth stumbling-blocks—which the contention of words is always wont to have—is struck and scandalized, so that it casts out and loses the word of faith which it had faintly conceived; and this is the quarrel and contention "unto the subversion of the hearers." If, therefore, the soul which has been scandalized casts out the word not yet formed, he who scandalized it is said to suffer loss. Do you wish to know that in some the word is formed, in some not yet formed? The word of the Apostle plainly teaches us, which we recalled above, when he says: "until Christ be formed in you"; but Christ is the Word of God. By this he shows that at the time when he was writing, the Word of God was not yet formed in them; if, therefore, it comes forth not yet formed, he shall suffer loss. Concerning the losses of teachers the Apostle also teaches, when he says: "but if anyone's work burns, he shall suffer loss. But he himself shall be saved, yet so as through fire." But the Lord too says in the Gospels: "for what does it profit a man, if he gain the whole world, but lose his own soul or suffer loss of it?" Whence it seems to be shown that certain sins pertain indeed to loss, yet not to destruction; because he who has suffered loss is nonetheless said to be saved—"he himself"—although "through fire." Whence, I believe, the Apostle John too in his epistle says that some sins are unto death, and some are not unto death. But what the kinds of sins unto death are, and what indeed "not unto death," but unto loss, I do not think can easily be discerned by any of men. For it is written: "who understands transgressions?" Nevertheless, from the things which are related in the Gospel through parables, we can in some part come to know of what sort those are which are named losses, since there we see certain things reckoned to gain which are said to have been acquired through trading. For example, when it is related that beyond five minas five others were acquired, or beyond two others two were acquired; or when a drachma or a denarius or a talent is set down and is named as a kind of money in the profit of works; but also when the householder is said to make a reckoning with his servants and there is offered to him one who owed ten thousand talents. Such, therefore, is a kind of reckoning of loss, so that, for example, one who was to receive ten minas for his wage receives not ten, but eight or six or even less; and he is said to be struck with this loss who has offered the occasion of stumbling to the weaker and womanly soul.

But he shall pay, it says, according to what "the woman's husband shall impose" or lay upon him, "and he shall pay with honor." The husband of the learning soul is its teacher; according, therefore, to what that husband shall impose—either Christ, who is the teacher of all, or he who in Christ's stead presides over the Church as teacher of souls—that man who "unto the subversion of the hearers" contends with words shall suffer loss for that soul which has cast out the "infant not yet formed." This can perhaps be taken of the scandal of a catechumen not yet formed. For it can come about that again the very one who caused the injury may instruct, repair, and restore to the soul the things which it lost, and may now do this "with honor," with modesty, with patience, as the Apostle says: "with meekness correcting those who resist"—not with quarreling, as before, when he brought in the scandal. "But if the infant be already formed, he shall give life for life." The "formed infant" can seem to be the word of God in the heart of that soul which has obtained the grace of baptism, or which has more plainly and more clearly conceived the word of faith. This soul, then, if, struck by the excessive contention of teachers, it casts out the word and is found to be of those of whom the Apostle spoke: "for already certain ones have turned back after Satan," "shall give life for life." Either it is to be understood as in the day of judgment before that judge "who is able to destroy both soul and body in Gehenna"; because elsewhere too the prophet says to Jerusalem: "I have given Egypt as your exchange, and Ethiopia and Syene for you." Or indeed perhaps this too can be fitted, that he who is conscious to himself of so great a scandal should lay down his own "life for the life" of that one whom he has scandalized, and should labor even unto death for how that one may return, may be repaired, may be restored to faith. Let him also lay down "eye for eye": if he has injured the eye of the soul, that is, has disturbed its understanding, let his own eye be taken from him by the one who presides over the Church, and let that turbulent and fierce understanding of his, which generates scandal, be cut away. But also if he has injured the tooth of the hearer, with which, receiving the food of the word, he was wont either to grind it small or to crush it with his molars, so as to transmit from these a refined sense to the belly of the soul—if he has vexed and torn out this tooth, so that by his contention the soul cannot subtly and spiritually receive the word of God, let the tooth be taken from him who does not rightly grind small and divide the foods of the Scriptures. For perhaps on this account it is said elsewhere too concerning the Lord: "you have shattered the teeth of sinners"; and elsewhere it is nonetheless written: "he who eats a sour grape, his teeth shall be set on edge"; and elsewhere: "the Lord has broken the grinding teeth of lions." Thus, therefore, the soul is said to be injured and struck through its members. "Hand" too "for hand" and "foot for foot" is demanded. The hand of the soul is the power by which it can hold and grip something, as if we should say its action and strength; and the foot is that by which it walks toward good things or bad. Because, therefore, if the soul suffers scandal, it is cast down not only in faith but also in acts, which are signified by the hands and feet, there are taken from him who offered the stumbling-block the hands with which he does not work rightly, and the feet with which he does not walk rightly. He shall also receive back the "burn" with which he burned and handed the soul over to Gehenna. By each of these particulars this is shown, that this striker, cut off in all his members, is to be excised from the body of the Church, "that the rest," it says, "seeing, may have fear and may not do likewise." Therefore the Apostle too, when he describes the teacher of the Church, among other things commands "not a striker," lest, striking pregnant women, souls just beginning, he lay down "life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth." Such also are those souls which the Lord too weeps over in the Gospels, when he says: "woe to those who are pregnant and nursing in those days," in which there shall be scandalized, "if it be possible, even the elect." Yet it should be known that it is not for the perfect to be scandalized, but either for women or for little ones, just as the Lord too says in the Gospel: "if anyone shall scandalize one of these least little ones." He, then, is little and least who can be scandalized: "but the spiritual man judges all things" and "tests all things and, what is good, holds fast, and abstains from every evil kind." These things, as far as they could occur to us, we have said in the present passage. But let us ask of the Lord that he himself may deign to reveal to us the things that are perfect, through Jesus Christ our Lord, "to whom be glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen."

CAN SOULS, THEN, BE TRANSLATED JUST LIKE BODIES? — I think it is dishonorable to say that souls are generated together with bodies, so that a soul is born from a soul, a thing that does not belong even to the soul itself. Or if indeed each of the heavenly powers was made individually, and from them the rest came to be, then it might seem believable that from the one soul of Adam the other souls are born. But this is not fitting, because this was possible for God alone, that the simple should generate, and was not granted to others. This is so mysterious in the case of the Savior that it is considered unbelievable not only by pagans or Jews alone, but even by those who call themselves Christians. For the Photinians and Arians reject this faith and do not believe that God has generated. For if at the time when the body is sown the soul also is generated from a soul, we read that a rib was taken from Adam, yet we do not read that a soul was born from a soul. But if the rib had a soul with it, then it was not born, but removed as a part. Yet this too is not written. The prophet Zechariah says among other things: “Who formed the spirit of man within him” (Zech. 12:1). Nor does Isaiah disagree with this, for he says: “Therefore says the Lord God who made you and formed you in the womb” (Isa. 44:2). If therefore it is formed in the womb, then it is given to an already shaped body. For when it fills all the members of the body, it is said to be fashioned in the body. Just as water, although without form, when poured into a vessel appears to be shaped, so the soul, though by nature incorporeal and simple, is as it were formed in the body, giving life to each of the members. Moses has handed this down more clearly, saying: “If someone strikes a woman who is pregnant in the womb, and she miscarries: if what is in her is fully formed, let him give soul for soul; but if it is unformed, let him be fined” (Exod. 21:22), so that he might prove that the soul is not present before the form. Therefore, if it is given to a body already formed, it is not born at the conception of the body, derived with the seed. For if the soul exists with the seed and comes from another soul, many souls perish every day, since the seed by a certain outflow does not come to birth. But if we look more closely, we shall see what we ought to follow. Let us consider the making of Adam. In Adam an example was given, so that from him it might be understood that a soul was received by an already formed body. For God could have mixed the soul with the clay of the earth and so have formed the body. But he proceeded with reason, because the house had first to be put together and then the inhabitant brought in. The soul, certainly, since it is spirit, cannot dwell in dryness; therefore it is carried in the blood. Consequently, when the features of the body have not yet been put together, where will the soul be? Does it wander outside until it is put in, although reason teaches that it is given in such a way as to animate the body, not to wander idly? But from whom is it given, let those who think otherwise tell us: from the male, or from the female? If from the female, it is not fitting, because the example is otherwise. For they propose that with the rib taken from the man, a soul was also given; and we have shown by many arguments that this is invalid. From this it might perhaps seem to be given from the female, especially on account of the Savior, whom we know to have been born of a woman from the Holy Spirit, without the union of flesh. But if they suppose this, they give more to women; for they transfer the authority of the man to the woman. Since they claim that the origin of both body and soul is from the man, they turn around and say that what is more important, namely the soul, is from the woman, and what is less, namely the body, is from the male; although it is clear that the order of the example given by God cannot be altered.

But what parts of the law can I defend as good with a greater confidence than those which heresy has shown such a longing for—as the statute of retaliation, requiring eye for eye, tooth for tooth and stripe for stripe? Now there is not here any smack of permission to mutual injury. There is rather, on the whole, a provision for restraining violence. To a people which was very obdurate and wanting in faith toward God, it might seem tedious and even incredible to expect from God that vengeance which was subsequently to be declared by the prophet: "Vengeance is mine; I will repay, says the Lord." Therefore, in the meanwhile, the commission of wrong was to be checked by the fear of retribution immediately to happen. So the permission of this retribution was to be the prohibition of provocation. In this way a stop might thus be put to all hot-blooded injury. By the permission of the second the first is prevented by fear. By this deterring of the first the second act of wrong fails to be committed.

Celsus does not quote any passages from the law which are apparently in contradiction to what stands in the gospel, so that we might compare them. He says, "And to a man who has struck one once one should offer oneself to be struck again." But we will say that we are aware that "it was said to them of old time, 'An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth,' " and that we have read also the words "But I say unto you, to him that strikes you on one cheek offer the other one also." However, I imagine that Celsus derived some of his vague notions from those who say that the God of the gospel is different from the God of the law and so made remarks like this. I would reply to his objection that the Old Testament also knows the doctrine that to him that strikes you on the right cheek you should offer the other one also. At any rate, it is written in the Lamentations of Jeremiah: "It is good for a man when he bears a yoke in his youth, he will sit alone and in silence when he has taken it on himself. He will give a cheek to the man who smites him and shall be filled with reproaches." The gospel then does not lay down laws in contradiction to the God of the law, not even if we interpret literally the saying about a blow on the jaw. And neither Moses nor Jesus "is wrong." Nor did the "Father forget when he sent Jesus the commands which he had given to Moses." Nor did he "condemn his own laws, and change his mind and send his messenger for the opposite purpose."

You have heard that it was said: An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth; but I say to you not to resist evil. He who says: An eye for an eye, does not wish to take away the other eye too, but to preserve both. Our Lord, taking away requital, cuts off the beginnings of sins. And in the law there is retribution, in the Gospel grace; there the fault is corrected, here the beginnings of sins are taken away.

Not to exceed due measure in inflicting punishment, lest the requital be greater than the injury—that is the lesser justice of the Pharisees. And it is a high degree of justice, for it would not be easy to find a man who, on receiving a fisticuff, would be content to give only one in return and who, on hearing one word from a reviler, would be content to return one word exactly equivalent. On the contrary, either he exceeds moderation because he is angry, or he thinks that, with regard to one who has inflicted an injury on another, justice demands a penalty greater than the injury suffered by the innocent person. To a great extent, such a spirit is restrained by the law, in which is written the directive, "An eye for an eye" and "A tooth for a tooth." Moderation is signified by these words, so that the penalty may not be greater than the injury. And this is the beginning of peace. But to have absolutely no wish for any such retribution—that is perfect peace.

Some think that the precepts of the Old Testament are stricter than those of the New; but these are certainly deceived by careless consideration. For in the Old Testament, not avarice but robbery is punished. There, property unjustly taken is punished by fourfold restitution. But here this rich man is not blamed for taking what belonged to others, but for not giving what was his own. Nor is it said that he oppressed anyone by violence, but that he exalted himself in the things he had received. From this, therefore, we must especially conclude with what punishment he should be punished who seizes what belongs to others, if he is struck with the condemnation of hell who does not share his own possessions. Therefore let no one consider himself safe, saying: "Behold, I do not seize what belongs to others, but I enjoy things lawfully granted to me," because this rich man was not punished for taking what belonged to others, but because he wrongly abandoned himself to the things he had received.

Watch therefore, for you do not know at what hour your Lord will come. Not giving "sleep to the eyes" of our soul nor "slumber to the eyelids," so that we may await either our own end or the end of the age, whether that we should depart from this life or that this world should be brought to its consummation for us.

But someone will ask how the Lord, established as present among the disciples, speaks thus, as though not present but about to come, saying to them: watch, for you do not know at what hour your Lord will come. And the one who is more simple will say that he spoke this discourse concerning the second coming, in which he was to come. But another will say that he was speaking of the intelligible coming of the Word, still to come into the understanding of the disciples, because it was not yet in their understanding in the way it was going to be: since (as he shows through this passage) in those who watch he works the day of his coming in the soul of those who are illumined by the true light of him who comes to their souls.

Now the householder is the understanding of the man, and his house is his soul; but the thief, who comes suddenly while the householder sleeps and breaks into the house, is, I think, the devil or every contrary word, according to what the evangelist John teaches us, saying in this manner: "amen amen I say to you, he who does not enter through the door into the sheepfold but climbs up another way, that man is a thief and a robber". As, therefore, he who "enters through the door into the sheepfold" is "the shepherd of the sheep", for whom "the doorkeeper opens", but "he who does not enter through the door but climbs up another way is a thief and a robber", so the lord of the house enters into it confidently "through the door" when he wills, rewarding the one who watches; but the thief, being a thief, does not enter into the house to the soul of the negligent by the natural entrance, but (as one who has already broken into it) first destroying certain natural buildings of his soul and natural understandings, in him who has not watched — the things which God the Word had built. And having entered through that very breach, the thief plunders it, disarming the understanding, when, despoiling the householder who does not watch, "he will distribute his spoils".

But sometimes someone catches the thief in the very act of breaking in, and seizing him as one having his own weapons, he strikes the thief, and, confuting the word that breaks in, he kills it, when, though killing, he is not reckoned a murderer, killing it without any delay. But if not in his own presence, yet in the presence of him who makes all hidden things manifest, someone catches him who has stolen his goods, and understands him and refutes him (that is, kills him), he has no pardon, the thief being dead and made manifest: for he too will die.

And see whether perhaps the law of Moses signifies some such thing, saying: "but if the thief is found in the very breaking in and, being struck, dies, there is no bloodguilt for him; but if the sun has risen over him, he is guilty: he shall die for it". For he who, before he does the evil, recognizes the evil and crushes it in himself, is the one who catches and kills it in himself, while it is being broken in upon by it. But he who, after he has done the evil, although he refutes it, is seen to have caught the evil outside himself and to have killed it outside his house — it profits him nothing, for he has been made guilty of death. For after any man has sinned and turned back into himself, the divine understanding which is in us illumines him like a light, so that we may understand that the evil we have committed was to our own condemnation, not to our salvation. Yet in the text of this Gospel of which we are speaking, the thief comes not by day, when the soul of the earnest man has been illumined by the sun of righteousness, but by night and in the time while malice still remains.

Some people give no thought to the question of demons, that is to say, to the fact that these demons, in order to be able to exist in the heavy atmosphere that encircles the earth, must have the nourishment of exhalations and consequently are always on the lookout for the savor of burnt sacrifices, blood and incense. Since they attach no importance to the matter of sacrifice, we would express ourselves also on this subject. If men who give sustenance to robbers, murderers and barbarian enemies of the great king are punished as criminals against the state, how much more will they be punished justly who through offering sacrifice proffer sustenance to the minions of evil and thus hold them in the atmosphere of the earth! And this holds true especially if knowing the text, "He that sacrifices to gods other than the Lord alone will be destroyed utterly," they nevertheless sacrifice to these authors of evil on earth. In my opinion, when there is question of crimes committed by these demons operating against men, they who sustain them by sacrificing to them will be held no less responsible than the demons themselves that do the crimes. By the law of Moses thecommand propounded to all the people generally was this: "Thou shalt offer to the Lord thy God thy tithes and firstfruits." And so, while we are commanded to offer tithes of our substance and all our fruits, it is much more needful for us to offer tithes of our life and ordinary employments and actions, which certainly is clearly arranged for in the calculation of Lent. For the tithe of the number of all the days included in the revolving circle of the year is thirty-six days and a half. But in seven weeks, if Sundays and Saturdays are subtracted, there remain thirty-five days assigned for fasting. But by the addition of Easter Eve when the Saturday's fast is prolonged to the cock-crowing at the dawn of Easter Day, not only is the number of thirty-six days made up, but in regard to the tithe of the five days which seemed to be over, if the bit of the night which was added be taken into account nothing will be wanting to the whole sum.

But what shall I say of the firstfruits which surely are given daily by all who serve Christ faithfully? For when men waking from sleep and arising with renewed activity after their rest, before they take in any impulse or thought in their heart, or admit any recollection or consideration of business consecrate their first and earliest thoughts as divine offerings, what are they doing indeed but rendering the firstfruits of their produce through the High Priest Jesus Christ for the enjoyment of this life and a figure of the daily resurrection? And also when roused from sleep in the same way they offer to God a sacrifice of joy and invoke Him with the first motion of their tongue and celebrate His name and praise, and throwing open, the first thing, the door of their lips to sing hymns to Him they offer to God the offices of their mouth; and to Him also in the same way their bring the earliest offerings of their hands anti steps, when they rise from bed and stand in prayer and before they use the services of their limbs for their own purposes, take to themselves nothing of their services, but for His glory advance their steps, and set them in His praise and so render the first fruits of all their movements by stretching forth the hands, bending the knees, and prostrating the whole body. For in no other way can we fulfil that of which we sing in the Psalm: "I prevented the dawning of the day and cried;" and: "Mine eves to Thee have prevented the morning that I might meditate on Thy words;" and: "In the morning shall my prayer prevent Thee;" unless after our rest in sleep when, as we said above, we are restored as from darkness and death to this light, we have the courage not to begin by taking any of all the services both of mind and body for our own uses. For there is no other morning which the prophet "prevented," or which in the same way we ought to prevent, except either ourselves, i.e., our occupations and feelings and earthly cares, without which we cannot exist-or the most subtle suggestions of the adversary, which he tries to suggest to us, while still resting and overcome with sleep, by the phantoms of vain dreams, with which, when we presently awake, he will fill our minds and occupy us, that he may be the first to seize and carry off the spoils of our firstfruits. Wherefore we must take the utmost care (if we want to fulfil in act the meaning of the above quoted verse) that an anxious watchfulness takes regard of our first and earliest morning thoughts, that they may not be defiled beforehand being hastily taken possession of by our jealous adversary, and thus he may make our firstfruits to be rejected by the Lord as worthless and common. And if he is not prevented by us with watchful circumspection of mind, he will not lay aside his habit of miserably anticipating us nor cease day after day to prevent us by his wiles. And therefore if we want to offer firstfruits that are acceptable and well pleasing to God of the fruits of our mind, we ought to spend no ordinary care to keep all the senses of our body, especially during the hours of the morning, as a sacred holocaust to the Lord pure and undefiled in all things. And this kind of devotion many even of those who live in the world observe with the utmost care, as they rise before it is light or very early, and do not at all mix in the ordinary and necessary business of this world before hastening to church and striving to consecrate in the sight of God the firstfruits of all their actions and doings.
